title: Song of the Jewel Mirror Samadhi, Part 2
speaker: Kanho Chris Burkhart
summary: The talk's main teaching emphasizes the importance of transforming not just our negative emotions and attachments, but their root causes as well. This requires a holistic approach that combines study, meditation, and guidance from a teacher, as well as letting go of ego-driven attitudes. Ultimately, true transformation leads to an experience of enlightenment that arises from our practice, embracing both the relative and absolute aspects of reality.

sentences.text: Good evening, everybody.
Thank you for being here for the second installment of the Jewel Mirror Samadhi.
Unless you've been to retreats or you come to our Saturday morning sit, you may not have heard this often.
It may sound a bit strange, very poetic, and you may wonder what it has to do with dharma.
A little bit about the background that I talked about last week: this poem is said to have been written by Dongshan, who was one of the founders of Soto Zen.
He lived in the ninth century, and he was the 38th ancestor in our lineage.
That said, it would be good if you looked at the poem as we're going through it.
It might help, since the language is not that easy to hold.
We got to the next lines that we are going to talk about:
*It is like the illumination hexagram, relative and ultimate interact.
Piled up, they make three.
The complete transformation makes five.
It is like the taste of the five-flavoured herb, like the diamond thunderbolt subtly included within the true.
Inquiry and response come up together.*
Now, I need to say something about that illumination hexagram.
"Piled up, they make three.
The complete transformation makes five."
That is straight out of the I Ching, of which I am absolutely 100% ignorant.
So I don't even want to go into the I Ching.
If you are curious about that, you can go into Google and look for the Jewel Mirror Samadhi translation study, and you will find a 100-page booklet that goes into great detail about this.
For the first time, we encounter this five.
"The transformation makes five.
It is like the taste of the five-flavoured herb, like a diamond thunderbolt," which, if you look at it, has five corners too.
And that is a riff on the five ranks that we briefly mentioned last time.
So Dongshan references the five levels of attainment, the five ranks.
They are used by the enlightened teacher to gauge the progress of a practitioner.
And another brief comment: I may say "vexations" a lot.
Vexations in this context means attachments, hindrances, and obstacles to your practice.
In this model of the five ranks, the vexations and wisdom interact in different ways.
Level one is called off-centre within the centre.
Usually that is shown as a circle with the top three-quarters solid black and the bottom white.
Most of the mental landscape is vexations, hindrances.
But there is this white underground, which shows the practitioner that there is wisdom, and even though there is a lot of vexation all over the place, there is a pretty solid practice already.
Level two is called centre within the off-centre.
That is usually shown as the same circle, most of it white and just a little bit of black at the bottom.
Wisdom dominates over vexation, and the practitioner is now really focused on getting rid of the last bottom black pool.
Level three, coming in the centre, is usually shown as a white circle with a little black dot in the middle.
Wisdom is not covered by wisdom, yet it continues to exist.
Vexations no longer manifest, but practice is still necessary.
Now number four, arrival with dual aspects.
It's a circle and it's all white.
In our conventional thinking we always say, "Hmm, this is where we want to go, right?
I did it!
All vexations have gone away."
What happens is that the wisdom disappears together with the vexations.
There is no more relationship, because wisdom, like vexations, only appears in the ordinary world of samsara.
If it's all white, there is no action, there is nothingness, emptiness, there are no more sentient beings and nobody to be saved.
So the highest level, according to Dongshan, is level five, perfection on both counts, or acquired wisdom.
It's usually shown as a circle that is all black.
This level fully relates to the world again.
It relates to the world of phenomena, and it uses vexations as wisdom to help sentient beings.
Because the practitioner no longer suffers from the vexations, she can fully use the vexations, the attachments and hindrances, to save sentient beings.
It could also be said that each one of those levels contains the other four, because, like we said last time, as soon as you say one, two pops up.
So the next lines:
*Communing with the source, travel the pathways, embrace the territory and treasure the road.
Respecting this is fortunate, do not neglect it.
Naturally real, yet inconceivable, it is not within the province of delusion or enlightenment.
With causal conditions, time and season, quiescently it shines bright.*
The source is the jewel mirror, the mind free from vexations or obstructions.
Traveling this road truly is a treasure.
"Naturally real" is Buddha nature, and "inconceivable" is the illumination of the jewel mirror, which is Buddha nature manifesting as wisdom.

One of the commentators, Sheng Yan, asks at this point that we do not mistake a state of naturalness, which is absolutely living in only what can be seen, heard, felt, tasted or smelled, for the jewel mirror.
If we are satisfied with this naturalness, we will have no concern for society and for others, for spiritual progress.
The light provided by the mirror together with naturalness, which is enlightenment, is ever present.
So we need the combination of the two.
Yet it does need to be realized.
Merit and wisdom are not created by our practice but, like the mirror cleared from dust, they are uncovered by practice, and thereby we provide the causal conditions.
Just like that, enlightenment does not sprout or ripen, because if it did, it would also be subject to death and decay.
The next two lines:
*In its fineness, it fits into spacelessness.
In its greatness, it is utterly beyond location.
A hairsbreadth deviation will fail to accord with the proper attunement.*
So we are talking about the world of the jewel mirror when we speak of spacelessness and greatness.
Sheng Yan again says that the enlightened mind does not move, yet it functions powerfully.
It is not hindered by attachments.
Our attachments and vexations truly limit us to seeing only what relates to our attachments.
The idea I have, or who or what I am, is a trap.
"Oh, I am not good at this" is a trap.
"He is smarter than I am" is a trap.
"I am faster than she is" is a trap.
Love is contentment with what is, without attachment to the outcome, not obsessing about morality while not indulging in evil.
The next lines are:
*Now there is sudden and gradual, in which teachings and approaches arise.
Once basic approaches are distinguished, then there are guiding rules.
But even though the basis is reached and the approach comprehended, true eternity still flows.*
Since that time there has been quibbling over sudden enlightenment and northern gradual cultivation.

Both the Jewel Mirror Samadhi and the merging of difference and unity speak against this kind of splitting apart, since we need both qualities, and each school has its own way, so there is no need to make an issue of right or wrong.
[unclear: "Kishit Saba"], [unclear: "Iron Rashi"] asked, "The sound of the bell, the raindrops on the roof, the water splashing along the gutter, where do they not meet?"
Rashi replied, "Bring me the mirror and I'll break it for you." [unclear: "Iron Rashi"] asked, "What does that mean?" [unclear: "Boko san Rashi"] answered, "Eternity still flows."
Partially, the Jewel Mirror Samadhi is a manual for teachers, how to look at their students' attainment.
Sometimes when we practice we really think we got it, and it's not it.
So the Jewel Mirror Samadhi also describes false enlightenment:
*Outwardly still, while inwardly moving, like a tethered colt, like a trapped rat, the ancient sages pitied them and bestowed upon them the teaching.*
In this spot I found Sheng Yan's translation very helpful.
He wrote:
*We still body but raising mind like a tethered horse or a mouse frozen by fright.
Past sages pitied them and liberated them with the Buddha Dharma.*
At times we may believe that we experience enlightenment because we hit this really nice place where we have lots of equanimity, things don't disturb us.
We have tamed that inner unrest.
We could call it a permanent samadhi.
Zen is not opposed to this samadhi.
However, attachment to samadhi is another attachment.
Since it is not true enlightenment, we just tamed the mind a bit.
It can break, and when conditions are not so good we might return to our comfortable old ways.
The mouse frozen by fright, it's still not because it's great, but it's just waiting for an opportunity to run off again.
I could tell you something about tethered horses but I don't have that much time.
Same story.
So if we take vexation and we change it, like we make it really small or really quiet or almost invisible, it's still there.
It's only the complete and utter transformation.
Change doesn't do it.
We need to totally transform it.
The next lines:
*According to their delusions they call black as white.
When erroneous imagination sees, the acquiescent mind realizes itself.*
Early Buddhism loved lists, and so there are four inverted views, or reversals of truth.
One, looking for the permanent in the impermanent.
Two, looking for ease in suffering.
Three, looking for the self in what is not the self.
Four, looking for the lovely in what is repulsive or impermanent.
Suchness alone lies outside of the range of erroneous imaginations.
Only the acquiescent mind can learn equally from all circumstances and all things.
The next lines are:
*If you want to conform to the ancient way, please observe the sages of former times.
When about to fulfill the way of Buddhahood, one gazed at a tree for ten eons.
Like a battle scarred tiger, like a horse with shanks gone gray.*
Here Dongshan encourages us to learn from the ancestors and to study the sutras.
Shakyamuni left many instructions and illuminated a path.
While Zen does not have the equivalent of the Bible, a holy book, the study of sutras is an important part of Zen practice.
It is a very recent attitude to not read sutras or to think that it is very Zen not to do so.
Through the study of sutras we can check our alignment with Buddha's teachings.
I can only see with the eye of my practice, of the person that I am, so we go astray and get caught by our own traps and detachments.
Along with the study of the sutras it is important to have a teacher who can help me see where my understanding is, and a teacher who can correct my mistakes.
The next lines, they've always really stumped me.
I couldn't see how they belonged there.
*Because there is the common, there are true pedestals, fine clothing.
Because there is the startlingly different, there are house cat and cow.*
These lines describe a student who practices and has not yet uncovered the true mirror.
He wears the Buddha's teaching like an external ornament.
So it asks us not to have a materialistic attitude towards practice.
Chokyam Trinpoche called it spiritual materialism: fancy temples, more robes, intricate ceremonies.
In other words, a big show of religion without spirituality is another dead end.
House cat and cow are very different in their behaviour and characteristics.
While they seem to be very different, we need a little bit of both in our practice.
Like the cat, we need to be clever and have understanding and balance.
And like the cow or the ox, we need to have solid [unclear: "train"] strength to be steady.
The next line:
*Yi with his archer skill could hit the target at 100 paces.
But when arrow points meet head on, what has this to do with the power of skill?*
Yi was an archer who was very famous for hitting his target dead on, but two arrows meeting mid-air is a different story.
When [unclear: "I lifted Trinpoche"], I asked Abbot Steve about these lines.
I said, "Hey, I don't get it."
And he laughed and said this one was easy.
When I reach an understanding, does it have to do with my careful thinking, or is it an experience?
Does enlightenment happen just because I finished the course or read the books?
No, it doesn't.
And yet practice, meditation and study do prepare the place for it to happen.
Yi needed his practice and skill, yet arrow points meeting in mid-air are not brought about by the power of skill.
But practice helps.
That's how one applies oneself.
The next lines are pretty interesting too:
*When the wooden man begins to sing, the stone woman gets up dancing.
It's not within reach.
A feeling of discrimination.
How could it admit of consideration in thought?*
Dogen said, sentient and insentient beings all have Buddha nature.
They are all Buddha from the same source.
No difference.
However, that insentient beings reach Buddhahood can only be understood through enlightenment.
Dogen wrote:

*Because earth, grass, trees, walls, tiles and pebbles all engage in Buddha activity, those who receive the benefit of wind and water caused by them are inconceivably helped by the Buddha's guidance, splendid and unthinkable, and awaken intimately to themselves.*
A wooden man may sing and it may be without sound.
When the stone woman gets up and dances, it very well may be without any movement at all.
Please don't use your imagination or special effects.
That's of no use.
*Ministers serve their lords.
Children obey their parents.
Not obeying is not filial.
Failure to serve is no help.
Just live right here and now, fulfilling your function to the fullest.*
Maybe these lines may offend those who don't like authoritarian systems.
To those, please keep in mind that at the time these lines were written, Dongshan was in a time and in a place where Confucian ideals were very strong.
In Confucian thought, well-ordered and correct hierarchy meant that the universe was in order, resolving in peace, perfection and well-being.
Offsetting this somewhat:
*Practice secretly, working within like a fool, like an idiot.
Just to continue in this way is called the host within the host.*
The great practitioner practices quietly toward Buddhahood.
She helps sentient beings.
He does not wish to become famous.
They find great benefit from practice and have great wisdom and compassion.
People may wish to call them a fool or think they're idiots, but that's okay.
It does not matter.
Let me end with the same summary that I read in the beginning.
Dongshan says that the world is made of two elements, sameness and difference.
The relative and the absolute are one.
As soon as you say one, there is no avoiding the two.
Salvation lies in no thought, which is freedom from discrimination and dichotomy.
All things obey one another.
True nature and the phenomenal world are meeting here and now, expressed as your life.
If you don't mind, I would like to finish this talk with a poem that Dongshan wrote about the five ranks.
*The apparent within the real: the third watch of the night before the moon appears.
No wonder when we meet there is no recognition.
Still cherished in my heart is the beauty of earlier days.*
*The real was in the apparent: a sleepy-eyed grandma encounters herself in an old mirror.
Clearly she sees a face, but it doesn't resemble her at all.
Too bad.
With a muddled head, she tries to recognize her reflection.*
*The coming from within the real: within nothingness, there is a path leading away from the dust of the world.
Even if you observe the taboo on the present emperor's name, you will surpass that eloquent one of yours who silenced every tongue.*
*The arrival at mutual integration: when two blades cross points, there is no need to withdraw.
The master swordsman is like the lotus blooming in the fire.
Such a man has in and of himself a heaven-soaring spirit.*
*Unity attained: who dares to equal him who falls into neither being nor non-being?
All men want to leave the current of ordinary life, but he after all comes back to sit among the coal and ashes.*
